title: Two Bins at Jazz on the Green: Innocent's Vote on Quitting
dek: In 1998 three friends spent £500 on fruit and asked festival-goers, by way of their empty bottles, whether they should give up their jobs.

story.founder: Richard Reed, Adam Balon, Jon Wright
story.event: Asking festival-goers at Jazz on the Green to vote with empty bottles on whether to quit their jobs
story.summary: In 1998 Richard Reed, Adam Balon and Jon Wright spent £500 on fruit and sold smoothies at Jazz on the Green, a small festival Reed and Balon ran at Parsons Green in west London, under a sign asking whether they should give up their jobs, with yes and no bins for the empties. The yes bin filled and they resigned straight afterwards. After months of refusals from banks and investors, an email asking friends for 'anyone rich' found Maurice Pinto, and Innocent began trading on 28 April 1999.
paragraphs: In 1998 three friends from Cambridge had good jobs in London: Richard Reed in advertising, Adam Balon in marketing for Virgin Cola, and Jon Wright as an engineering consultant. Their diets were poor; it was all "pizza, kebab or burger", Wright said later. On a snowboarding holiday that February they decided to stop talking about starting a business and start one. They settled on fruit smoothies. All three already owned juicers.

What they knew, Balon admitted, was "absolutely nothing about fruit". Leaving secure jobs was a big step, so before anyone resigned they wanted the idea tested on strangers. Reed and Balon already ran a small music festival, Jazz on the Green, at Parsons Green in west London; its third year fell in September 1998, by the Irish Times's account. They spent £500 on fruit, and a carrot farmer with a fruit press and a bottling line helped them make enough drinks for a stall, sold at £1.80 each.

Above the stall went a big sign: "Do you think we should give up our jobs to make these smoothies?" In front stood two bins, one marked yes and one marked no, and customers were asked to vote with their empty bottles. By the end of the weekend the yes bin was full. In Balon's telling, the three told each other they were doing it now, and promptly resigned: the next day, by the company's account, or the following Monday, by his.

The vote turned out to settle less than it seemed. In Balon's account, they quickly found how much about running a business they still had to learn. The company later wrote that they rewrote the business plan eleven times and that every bank, venture capitalist and business angel in London turned them down; Wright recalled investors chasing internet companies, not fruit juice. A last email to everyone they knew asked whether anyone knew anyone rich. It reached Maurice Pinto, an American businessman, who put in £230,000 by Balon's account, or £250,000 in later reports.
On 28 April 1999, the first day of business, Wright sold the first three cases to a local sandwich bar. Years later Reed's advice was blunt: "If you're 70% sure about an idea then go for it."

quote.text: Though a dress presented by the sovereign be honorable, yet is our own tattered garment preferable; and though the viands at a great man's table be delicate, yet is our own homely fare more sweet
quote.locator: Chapter VIII (Of the Duties of Society), maxim LXXXIX
quote.source_title: The Persian Literature, Volume 2 (The Gulistan, tr. James Ross), Project Gutenberg eBook #13060
quote.connection: Saadi prefers your own worn garment to a sovereign's gift, and your own plain food to a great man's table. The sign over the stall put that question to strangers: was a small thing of their own making worth more than secure places in other people's firms?

reflection: It is tempting to read the full bin as proof. It was not quite that: a festival crowd enjoying a cold drink on a weekend is not a shop reordering stock, and the founders learned the difference in the months of refusals that followed. What the bins did was make the decision visible, to themselves and to each other, and give them a day on which to act.
You do not need a crowd for that. Sometimes it is enough to put the question in plain words where you and the people you trust can see it, and to agree when you will answer it.
invitation: Write the decision you keep circling as one plain yes-or-no question, and ask one person whose judgement you trust to answer it today, with one reason.

research_notes: Pinto's money: Balon (MoneyWeek, 2006) said Pinto gave them £230,000; the Guardian (2009) and the Irish Times (2008, which says he 'lent' it) give £250,000. The story gives both, attributed. Festival date: the Irish Times says the third Jazz on the Green was in September 1998; Balon says 'the summer of 1998' and the Guardian 'that summer's day'; approx_date uses 1998-09 and the story attributes September to the Irish Times. Resignation timing: the company's timeline and website (quoted by the Irish Times) say they resigned the next day; Balon says the following Monday; both are given. An Inc. article (blocked to the verifier, so not cited or read in full) reportedly has Balon describing a coin toss after the vote; because I could not read it, the story does not mention it. Launch: the company's timeline gives 28 April 1999 as the first day of business; Balon says they were up and running in May 1999; the story uses the company's dated account. Founding year: BBC 2009 says the firm was set up in 1999, BBC 2010 says 1998, and the Guardian's 2016 Observer interview says Reed quit his job in 1999 at 26; this last conflicts with both founders' own accounts of resigning straight after the 1998 festival, so the story follows the founders. Wright's job: the Irish Times says engineering consultant; BBC 2010 says two of the three went into management consultancy; the story uses the Irish Times. Number of refusals: the company says every bank, VC and angel in London; Balon says 20 bank branches; neither number is relied on beyond attribution. Wikipedia's claim that only three bottles went in the 'no' bin is unsourced and not used. Funding is 'mixed': the test was paid for by the founders themselves, the company by a private investor. The company timeline is cited from an Internet Archive copy over http, because web.archive.org refused https connections intermittently during checking.
